recent_posts.title: Why replacing software homepages with chat boxes shifts complexity to users
recent_posts.summary: A critique of the growing trend of replacing enterprise software homepages with AI prompt/chat boxes. The argument is that empty text inputs don't simplify software — they displace complexity from product teams onto users. Structured UIs provide affordances and enable muscle memory; blank boxes provide no guidance. Suggested prompts bolted onto these interfaces are a tacit admission that the blank box alone is insufficient. Chat interfaces work well for exploratory queries, one-off actions, and onboarding, but shouldn't be the primary interface. The best enterprise software succeeds by making a strong opinion about the user's primary job and building the default experience around it. The real challenge is understanding users deeply enough to surface the right interface at the right moment — intent-first design rather than chat-first or dashboard-first.

recent_posts.title: Solari split-flap
recent_posts.summary: A browser-based Solari split-flap display built with vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no frameworks, no build step, just a single HTML file. Each cell simulates a physical drum that spins forward through characters in sequence, decelerating as it reaches the target, with synthesized mechanical click sounds via the Web Audio API. Quotes cycle every 5 seconds with staggered cascade animations. The project is open-source and MIT-licensed on GitHub, and was initially built in minutes using Claude.

recent_posts.title: When Meta Became the Work
recent_posts.summary: Large companies have spent years promoting people who excel at representing work rather than doing it, creating a systemic bias toward process, documentation, and stakeholder management over actual building and shipping. AI has now made this a crisis: small teams can attack established markets faster and cheaper than ever, while large orgs remain trapped in planning cycles, layered approvals, and cultures that actively reject the decisive, action-oriented people they now desperately need. The path forward requires rewarding builders again, compressing idea-to-ship timelines to weeks, treating direct market feedback as the primary input to decisions, and maintaining a consistent shipping cadence. Companies that fail to do this will drift further from their markets until the gap is too wide to close.

recent_posts.title: 16 reflections on design craft and career longevity
recent_posts.summary: A senior designer shares 16 personal reflections on the craft and career of design. Key themes include: creativity stemming from love and courage rather than talent, the importance of capturing ideas immediately, treating designs as vehicles for conversation rather than final artifacts, the value of cross-disciplinary exposure over staying within design circles, reframing feedback as dialogue, and the critical role of consistency and resilience for long-term career longevity. The piece emphasizes that polish, alignment, and the ability to bring others along on a creative journey matter as much as raw design skill.

recent_posts.title: New Claude Skill: Stop Slop
recent_posts.summary: Stop Slop is a skill file for Claude Code (and compatible tools like Cursor) that detects and eliminates common AI writing patterns from prose. It targets overused phrases ('Here's the thing', 'Let that sink in'), formulaic sentence structures, and repetitive habits like always using three examples or ending sections with punchy one-liners. The skill also includes a 1-10 scoring system across five dimensions—directness, rhythm, trust, authenticity, and density—with a threshold of 35/50 before revising. Available on GitHub under MIT license.

recent_posts.title: Why designers need more exposure beyond the design community
recent_posts.summary: Designers limit their effectiveness by spending too much time with other designers instead of broadening their exposure to different perspectives. Cross-functional conversations with PMs, engineers, sales, and customer support reveal context that pure design discussions never surface. Creativity in design comes from connecting disparate ideas and understanding user realities, which requires actively seeking out diverse inputs. Broad exposure to business context, market dynamics, and user problems is what separates designers who consistently produce effective work from those who produce only polished but misaligned output.

recent_posts.title: Introducing Vibe Slack
recent_posts.summary: Vibe Slack is an open-source, pixel-perfect Slack clone prototype built entirely with Cursor, designed for product teams who need to demo integrations in a realistic Slack environment. A setup wizard (`npm run setup`) generates a fully contextual workspace in seconds by asking 10 questions about company name, industry, size, and team composition. It auto-generates industry-appropriate channels, realistic conversation history, team members with distinct messaging styles, and an AI assistant. Key features include real-time message streaming with smart throttling, four visual themes, rich emoji reactions, presence indicators, file embeds (Loom, Figma, Confluence, Notion, Jira), and third-party workflow connectors. The project is open-source and forkable.

recent_posts.title: Vibe Prototyping & Cursor
recent_posts.summary: A product designer at Atlassian shares practical lessons from 60+ hours of vibe coding using Cursor, spending roughly 1.5 billion tokens building an elaborate interactive prototype without ever opening Figma. The post covers why Cursor stands out over tools like Lovable, Bolt, and Replit, then provides a detailed set of best practices: using Git commits as snapshots, defining project taxonomy early, using @ file references in prompts, managing context window rot by starting fresh chats, populating prototypes with real data, reviewing AI plans before executing large edits, structured prompt formats, and key Cursor configuration tips like model switching, agent mode, and dependency locking. The piece closes with a vision that the future of design will be built in code rather than drawn on canvases.

recent_posts.title: Fast is a Moat
recent_posts.summary: Speed — the ability to turn ideas into tangible results quickly — is framed as the most powerful competitive moat for designers and ambitious individuals. The argument is that fast execution isn't about rushing or sacrificing quality; quality is the baseline, speed is the advantage layered on top. Prototyping ideas quickly makes them real, drives alignment, and seizes ownership. Fast operators produce more output, attract more opportunity, and stay ahead of the curve rather than reacting to problems. The core mindset shift: obsess over priorities, not deadlines.

recent_posts.title: Generative UI and Early Thoughts
recent_posts.summary: Generative UI proposes replacing deterministic, hard-coded interfaces with LLM-driven layouts generated at runtime based on user context and intent. Rather than designers pre-defining every possible UI state, a design grammar and intent description are provided, and the model produces the most relevant interface structure dynamically. A simple tab navigation example illustrates the contrast between static and generative approaches, highlighting how this shifts product design from upfront scenario prediction to real-time adaptation.
